---
title: "Migrating from vitae"
subtitle: "Moving an R Markdown CV from the vitae R package to Quarto vitae"
engine: markdown
---

::: {.callout-note}
## Written for people and agents

This guide is written to be followed by a person or by an LLM coding agent. The
easiest way to migrate a CV from the vitae R Markdown templates is to open your
CV project with an agent and point it here:

> Migrate my CV to Quarto vitae by following
> <https://quarto-vitae.github.io/migration.html>

Agents should work through the [checklist](#checklist) at the end of this page.
Each step rewrites one construct and never changes the CV's content. Render after
migrating and compare the PDF page by page with the old one.
:::

The [vitae](https://pkg.mitchelloharawild.com/vitae/) R package built CVs from
R Markdown, with entries produced by `detailed_entries()`, `brief_entries()` and
`bibliography_entries()`. Quarto vitae keeps the same idea — a CV is data plus a
layout — but the layout is chosen with cell options rather than R functions, so
the data no longer has to come from R.

Most CVs migrate with mechanical changes: the data in your `tribble()`s stays as
it is, and only the code around it changes. This page walks through each change,
using the Awesome CV template as the worked example.

## At a glance

| vitae (R Markdown)                          | Quarto vitae                                                     |
|---------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `CV.Rmd`                                    | `CV.qmd`                                                         |
| `output: vitae::awesomecv`                  | `format: awesomecv-pdf`                                          |
| `keep_tex: true` under `output`             | `keep-tex: true` at the top level                                |
| `email:`, `github:`, `address:` …           | a `social:` list                                                 |
| ``date: "`r format(Sys.time(), '%B, %Y')`"`` | `date: today` with `date-format: "MMMM, YYYY"`                   |
| `library(vitae)`                            | not needed                                                       |
| `detailed_entries(what, when, with, where, why)` | `#| vitae:` cell option with `style: detailed`              |
| `brief_entries(what, when, with)`           | `#| vitae:` cell option with `style: brief`                      |
| `bibliography_entries("refs.bib")`          | `::: {.entries style="bibliography" file="refs.bib"}`            |
| list column of bullet points                | one row per bullet, merged with `collapse: why`                  |
| `glue("\\textbf{<x>}")`, `.protect = FALSE` | markdown (`**x**`); escaping is automatic                        |
| `\\newline` inside an entry                 | `` `\newline`{=latex} ``                                         |
| `\newpage`, `\begin{cvparagraph}`           | unchanged — raw LaTeX still works                                |
| `rmarkdown::render("CV.Rmd")`               | `quarto render CV.qmd`                                           |

## 1. Install the template

Templates are Quarto extensions, installed into your project rather than into R:

```bash
quarto add quarto-vitae/awesome-cv
```

This creates `_extensions/quarto-vitae/awesomecv/`. Commit it, so the CV renders
the same way on any machine.

vitae copied the template's class file and fonts next to your document (for
Awesome CV, `awesome-cv.cls` and `fonts/`). These are no longer used and can be
deleted. If your `.gitignore` names them, anchor the patterns to the project root
(`/awesome-cv.cls`), otherwise they will also hide the copy inside
`_extensions/`.

Rendering still needs a LaTeX installation with xelatex; fonts are fetched on the
first render.

## 2. Rename the document

Rename `CV.Rmd` to `CV.qmd`. Using `git mv` keeps the file's history:

```bash
git mv CV.Rmd CV.qmd
```

R code cells keep working: Quarto runs them with knitr, as before.

## 3. Rewrite the front matter

Before:

```yaml
---
name: Marie Curie
date: "`r format(Sys.time(), '%B, %Y')`"
position: Physicist
address: Paris, France
email: marie.curie@example.org
website: example.org
github: mcurie
linkedin: mcurie
headcolor: "414141"
output:
  vitae::awesomecv:
    keep_tex: true
---
```

After:

```yaml
---
name: Marie Curie
position: Physicist
social:
  - address: Paris, France
  - email: marie.curie@example.org
  - website: example.org
  - github: mcurie
  - linkedin: mcurie
headcolor: "414141"
date: today
date-format: "MMMM, YYYY"
show_footer: true
format: awesomecv-pdf
---
```

The changes:

- **`output` becomes `format`**, named `<template>-pdf`. Format options such as
  `keep-tex` move to the top level (or under `format:`), spelt with hyphens.
- **Contact details move into `social`**, a list shown in the order written. The
  keys are the same service names vitae used (`email`, `phone`, `github`,
  `linkedin`, `orcid`, …). `social` is shared by every Quarto vitae template; see
  [Contact details](using-templates.qmd#contact-details-and-profiles).
- **Use Quarto's date handling** instead of inline R in the YAML.
- **Check which options your template reads.** vitae's templates read a fixed set
  of fields; Quarto templates document their own. In Awesome CV the footer is
  now opt-in (`show_footer: true`), `name` and `surname` are separate (a
  `surname` is set in bold, so leave it out to keep a single-weight name), and
  `qualifications` is not used.

## 4. Remove the vitae package

Delete `library(vitae)` from the setup cell. Keep any other packages you use to
build the data, such as the tidyverse.

## 5. Convert `detailed_entries()`

vitae took the columns as arguments in a fixed order: `what`, `when`, `with`,
`where`, `why`. In Quarto vitae the cell simply prints a data frame, and a
`vitae` cell option says how to lay it out. `fields` renames your columns to the
template's field names, written `new: old`.

Before:

````markdown
```{r}
tribble(
  ~ role, ~ company, ~ loc, ~ dates, ~ details,
  "Professor", "University of Paris", "Paris", "1906-1934",
    list("First woman to hold the chair", "Directed the Curie Laboratory"),
) %>%
  detailed_entries(role, dates, company, loc, details)
```
````

After:

````markdown
```{r}
#| vitae:
#|   style: detailed
#|   collapse: why
#|   fields: {what: role, when: dates, with: company, where: loc, why: details}
tribble(
  ~ role, ~ company, ~ loc, ~ dates, ~ details,
  "Professor", "University of Paris", "Paris", "1906-1934",
    list("First woman to hold the chair", "Directed the Curie Laboratory"),
) %>%
  mutate(details = map(details, unlist)) %>%
  unnest_longer(details)
```
````

Turn the positional arguments into `fields` directly:
`detailed_entries(A, B, C, D, E)` becomes
`fields: {what: A, when: B, with: C, where: D, why: E}`. Leave out any
argument you did not pass.

**Bullet points.** A data frame prints as a table, and a table cell cannot hold
a list. Unnest the list column so each bullet is its own row, then set
`collapse: why`: consecutive rows that differ only in `why` are merged back into
one entry. The `map(details, unlist)` step is needed when some entries give a
single string rather than a `list()`, which `unnest_longer()` otherwise rejects.

## 6. Convert `brief_entries()` {#brief-entries}

The same pattern applies, but **check how your template lays out a brief entry**,
because the field that each argument lands in can change.

In vitae's Awesome CV, `brief_entries(what, when, with)` set `what` in regular
weight and put `with` in the right-hand column. In Quarto vitae's Awesome CV,
`what` is set in **bold**, `with` follows it after a comma, and the right-hand
column is `where`. To keep the same layout, map the old `with` to `where`:

````markdown
```{r}
#| vitae:
#|   style: brief
#|   fields: {what: award, when: year, where: from}
tribble(
  ~ award, ~ from, ~ year,
  "Nobel Prize in Chemistry", "Swedish Academy", "1911",
)
```
````

The layout each style uses is in the template's `entries/<style>.tex` file, under
`_extensions/`, and in its README.

## 7. Replace LaTeX in entries with markdown

vitae passed entry text to LaTeX, so CVs often built it with `glue()` and
`.protect = FALSE`. Quarto vitae reads entry text as **markdown** and escapes
LaTeX special characters itself.

| vitae                                 | Quarto vitae                             |
|---------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `\\textbf{x}`                         | `**x**`, or the field the template bolds |
| `\\emph{x}`                           | `*x*`                                    |
| `\\url{https://…}`                    | `<https://…>`                            |
| `\\&`, `5\\%`                         | `&`, `5%`                                |
| `.protect = FALSE`                    | not needed                               |
| `\\newline`                           | `` `\newline`{=latex} ``                 |

Manual escapes such as `\\&` are no longer needed. They happen to be harmless,
since a backslash before punctuation is also a markdown escape, but other LaTeX
commands are not: `\\textbf{x}` prints as the literal text.

A common vitae idiom bolded a title inside one long string, such as
`glue("\\textbf{<title>}: <details>")`. Now that `brief` bolds `what` itself,
split the string across fields instead:

```r
transmute(what = title, with = details, when)
```

The result reads `**title**, details` rather than `**title**: details` — the
separator is the template's.

**Line breaks.** Where an entry needs a line break inside it, use pandoc's raw
LaTeX syntax. Pad it with spaces, so it is not glued to the next word:

```r
br <- " `\\newline`{=latex} "
transmute(what = pkg, with = paste(role, br, details), when = paste0(year, br))
```

Adding `br` to the date, as vitae CVs often did, keeps the date level with the
first line of a two-line entry.

## 8. Convert `bibliography_entries()`

Bibliographies are a fenced div pointing at the file, with no code cell:

```markdown
::: {.entries style="bibliography" file="publications.bib"}
:::
```

The references are formatted by citeproc rather than biblatex, so the citation
style changes: by default they are listed alphabetically, author–date. Set `csl:`
in the front matter to choose a style; for a reverse-chronological list:

```yaml
csl: https://www.zotero.org/styles/apa-cv
```

To filter a bibliography, read it in R and print CSL back out from a cell with
`style: bibliography`; see the
[curriculum documentation](https://github.com/quarto-vitae/curriculum#bibliographies).

## 9. Keep raw LaTeX as it is

`\newpage` and the template's own environments, such as Awesome CV's
`cvparagraph`, work unchanged:

```latex
\begin{cvparagraph}
I have taught applied forecasting for ten years, in the top 5\% of units.
\end{cvparagraph}
```

Text inside a raw LaTeX environment is still LaTeX, so its escapes stay. To write
markdown inside one, open and close it with raw blocks:

````markdown
```{=latex}
\begin{cvparagraph}
```
I have taught applied forecasting for ten years, in the top 5% of units.
```{=latex}
\end{cvparagraph}
```
````

## 10. Render and compare

```bash
quarto render CV.qmd
```

Compare the result with your old PDF. Expect small differences from the updated
template, such as icons, font sizes and the separator in brief entries. Larger
differences usually mean a field landed in the wrong place; see
[step 6](#brief-entries).

## Checklist {#checklist}

1. `quarto add quarto-vitae/<template>`; delete the old copied class file and
   `fonts/`; anchor any `.gitignore` patterns for them with a leading `/`.
2. `git mv CV.Rmd CV.qmd`.
3. Front matter: `output:` → `format: <template>-pdf`; contact keys → `social:`
   list; inline-R `date` → `date: today` + `date-format`; add options the new
   template needs (Awesome CV: `show_footer: true`); drop unused ones.
4. Remove `library(vitae)`.
5. Each `detailed_entries(A, B, C, D, E)` → print the data frame, with
   `#| vitae: {style: detailed, fields: {what: A, when: B, with: C, where: D, why: E}}`.
   If `why` is a list column, add `collapse: why` and unnest it
   (`mutate(x = map(x, unlist)) %>% unnest_longer(x)`).
6. Each `brief_entries(A, B, C)` → `style: brief`, mapping each argument to the
   field the *new* template shows where the old one showed it (Awesome CV:
   `{what: A, when: B, where: C}`).
7. Replace `glue()` LaTeX with markdown; drop `.protect = FALSE` and manual
   escapes (`\\&`, `\\%`, optional but tidier); `\\newline` → `` " `\\newline`{=latex} " ``.
8. `bibliography_entries("f.bib")` → `::: {.entries style="bibliography" file="f.bib"}`
   `:::`, and choose a `csl:` if order or style matters.
9. Leave `\newpage` and raw LaTeX environments alone.
10. `quarto render`, then compare each page with the old PDF.

## Troubleshooting

`Can't combine <list> and <character>` from `unnest_longer()`
: Some entries give one string and others a `list()`. Normalise them first with
  `mutate(details = map(details, unlist))`.

`Undefined control sequence` mentioning `\newlineSomething`
: A raw `\newline` was pasted directly against the next word. Put spaces around
  it.

Literal LaTeX such as `\textbf{…}` printed in the CV
: Entry text is markdown now. Replace LaTeX commands with markdown, or wrap
  them as `` `\cmd`{=latex} ``.

Entries render but a column is missing or in the wrong place
: The field names differ between templates. Check the template's
  `entries/<style>.tex` for the fields it uses, and adjust `fields`.

See also the general [troubleshooting](using-templates.qmd#troubleshooting) for
writing a CV.
